items.title: Boy, 7, pulled alive from rubble hours after Russian strike on Ukraine, rescuers say
items.summary: Ten people are dead in the attack on Dymer, with rescue efforts ongoing to find those still missing from the residential building.
items.body:
Figure caption,

'Danger seems greater all the time': Ukrainians search for missing after Russian strikes hit Kyiv

ByHafsa Khalil

Updated 33 minutes ago

ByJessica Lamb

A seven-year-old boy has been rescued from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer after 14 hours, in overnight Russian strikes on Dymer, in the Kyiv region, that killed nine people, Ukrainian officials have said.

The attack occurred in the early hours of Sunday. A 79-year-old woman was also rescued alive from the collapsed building, Kyiv's regional head Tymur Tkachenko said.

A strike on a private home in Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 wounded in a separate strike on Vyshneve, also in the Kyiv region, that hit a grocery store on Sunday.

Ukrainian authorities said the boy in Dymer is in stable condition and was taken to hospital, and have thanked everyone involved in saving his life.

Zelensky and Ukraine's national police also confirmed the rescue of the boy.

Response teams including police, explosive technicians, dog handlers and medics are continuing with rescue efforts.

In a telegram post, Tkachenko said the 79-year-old woman rescued from the rubble was receiving treatment in hospital.

Earlier he said six people were injured in the attack, while others were still missing.

Image source, Ukraine State Emergency Service

Image caption,

The attack on the residential building occurred in the early hours of the morning while people were asleep

Zelensky said more than 130 people are involved in emergency operations at the scene, and that they will continue until they have "complete information about every single person".

Sending his condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed, he said the strike struck the residential building, "practically blowing a section of it to smithereens".

Zelensky added that "rescue efforts are complicated by constant new air raid alerts and renewed threats".

The strike hit the building at 05:00 local time, when families were still asleep, Ukraine's minister of internal affairs Ivan Vyhivskyi said.

More than 70 strikes have been launched across 10 Ukrainian regions as of Sunday evening, Vyhivskyi added.

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Emergency workers continue to search for those missing after Russian drone and missile attacks in Dymer.

In his video address posted online, Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 injured in a strike on an "ordinary grocery store" in Vyshneve.

Tkachenko previously said two other people were killed and eight wounded in the Vyshneve attack.

Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukraine's Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said in a post on X., external

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

items.summary: Crown says accused developed ‘jealous obsession’ but defence says ‘he was a poorly behaved boyfriend’ Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Love made a fool of Beau Lamarre-Condon, but it did not make him a murderer, h…
items.body:
Beau Lamarre-Condon was driven by jealous obsession when he drove to Jesse Baird’s house and shot him, the prosecution has alleged. Photograph: Rocco Fazzari/AAP

Beau Lamarre-Condon was driven by jealous obsession when he drove to Jesse Baird’s house and shot him, the prosecution has alleged. Photograph: Rocco Fazzari/AAP

Beau Lamarre-Condon ‘executed’ Jesse Baird and Luke Davies then lied about it, prosecution argues

Crown urges jury to reject accused’s claim of self-defence and find him guilty of murdering Sydney couple

• Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updates

• Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Beau Lamarre-Condon is a “proven and persistent liar” and the evidence in his double murder trial shows the deaths of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies could only have been an “execution”, a court has been told.

Lamarre-Condon is accused of fatally shooting the Sydney couple with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.

The former officer has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter, claiming the two men died while he acted in “self-defence”.

Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC urged the jury to reject Lamarre-Condon’s account and convict him on all three counts, as he wrapped up his closing statement on Monday.

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email

Driven by his jealous obsession, the accused drove to Paddington in a hired car, waited for his opportunity, entered the house with a gun loaded with stolen bullets, and shot Baird in the back and temple, Hatfield alleged.

“It was not self-defence or an accident,” he told the New South Wales supreme court.

“The evidence speaks only to an execution.”

Lamarre-Condon had testified he shot Baird after he lunged at him with a knife.

During this struggle, his gun was then flung across the room and picked up by Davies before the officer grabbed his arm and pushed the gun towards Davies.

Davies then pulled the trigger and shot himself, Lamarre-Condon told the court.

But this defence rests entirely on his own account and even if Baird had picked up a knife, it would not have assisted him against a glock, Hatfield said.

“You might think he is a proven and persistent liar and such a scenario is completely contrary to the weight of the evidence,” he told the court.

“The accused’s account is not the truth. It is a story made up after the fact in an attempt to meet the evidence.”

The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

items.summary: Coalition calls for climate change minister to resign immediately or be sacked over ‘catastrophic diplomatic disaster’, despite offering no alternatives on reducing emissions Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here Anthony Albanese has defended Chris B…
items.body:
Anthony Albanese and Chris Bowen (R) earlier this month at a Cop31 event. Bowen said despite a breakdown in negotiations, the transition away from fossil fuels is inevitable. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP

Anthony Albanese and Chris Bowen (R) earlier this month at a Cop31 event. Bowen said despite a breakdown in negotiations, the transition away from fossil fuels is inevitable. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP

‘Difficult geopolitical times’: Albanese defends Bowen after Cop31 deal failure

Coalition calls for climate change minister to resign immediately or be sacked over ‘catastrophic diplomatic disaster’, despite offering no alternatives on reducing emissions

• Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here

Anthony Albanese has defended Chris Bowen from criticism following the failure of the UN Cop31 climate summit, blaming the result on “difficult geopolitical times” as the Coalition called for the minister to resign.

Bowen served as president of negotiations at the talks in Turkey, helping run the conference with his Turkish counterpart, Murat Kurum.

Speaking to journalists late on Sunday after a list of countries rejected a proposed “cover decision” – an overarching agreement – for the conference, Bowen said “Australia left nothing on the field” but the “red lines” he and his staff tried to negotiate to find consensus between nearly 200 countries were unbridgeable.

Cop31 failed but in ‘the real world’ the transition away from fossil fuels is inevitable

Read more

The biggest sticking point was whether the agreement would mention the need for the world to transition away from fossil fuels. The European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, Norway and Belize told the conference they would not accept a deal without it.

Saudi Arabia and Russia led a group of oil-rich countries that vowed to veto a decision that included mention of fossil fuels.

Bowen told reporters: “I would have been happy with [a] transition away from fossil fuels being in the text, but that was not going to get support.”

He said despite the breakdown, “in the real world” the transition away from fossil fuels was inevitable and happening at speed. He said more than 90 countries had signed a pledge to increase electrification to 35% by 2035 – a step that should help cut fossil fuel use if delivered – but acknowledged the result was “very disappointing”.

Australia was sharply criticised during the conference for its continued support for new coal and gas export developments. Speaking on Monday, Albanese said Australia’s efforts had been critical in building relationships with Pacific neighbours.

“It’s evidence that we’re living in difficult geopolitical times,” he said of the result. “That is the reality. The important work of Cop is the work that we’ve done with the Pacific, where Australia and our Pacific leaders have worked constructively together.

“In order to have credibility [in the Pacific], the entry fee is action on climate change.”

The Coalition’s energy spokesperson, Dan Tehan, said Bowen should “resign immediately”.

“If Chris Bowen does not resign immediately, the prime minister should sack him,” Tehan said. “As the lead negotiator, Chris Bowen is personally responsible for this catastrophic diplomatic disaster.”

The Greens’ deputy leader, Steph Hodgins-May, said it was a “disastrous embarrassment” that Australia had chaired negotiations over the failed deal. In a statement, she said Labor was “not fit to lead – not on the world stage for climate negotiations, and not at home when it comes to protecting Australians from climate destruction”.

The Coalition, and Tehan specifically, have consistently attacked Labor’s bid to host the conference and Bowen’s installation as president of negotiations. Bowen argued for the role – newly created for Cop31 – after Turkey won the hosting rights after a protracted stand0ff.

Tehan did not say what the Coalition would have done differently if he was in Bowen’s shoes, other than saying the opposition would not have pursued hosting Cop or the position of president of negotiations. The Coalition has abandoned its support for Australia reaching net zero emissions by 2050 – a target introduced under former Liberal prime minister Scott Morrison – and promised to abolish Labor’s climate policies if elected.

It has not put forward any policies to reduce emissions.

Tehan said the consensus model of agreement used at the UN summit was “completely and utterly broken”. “Chris Bowen should have known that,” he said.

skip past newsletter promotion

after newsletter promotion

While the failure to get countries to agree to the “Antalya pact” in Turkey was a significant moment in the history of UN climate summits, the talks did not collapse completely.

The sticking point was the attempt to find language to reflect the “transition away for fossil fuels” that had been agreed to in 2023 in Dubai.

In the final stages of the talks, countries were presented with a text that only referred back to that decision and did not explicitly say “fossil fuels” – infuriating a sweep of countries.

Cop31 left Chris Bowen stuck between petrostates and climate reality. But the f-word failure is not his alone

Read more

Bill Hare, the Australian chief executive of Climate Analytics and a Cop veteran, said the lack of agreement on the main document at Cop31 – there was consensus on some minor issues – should not be seen as a failure of the entire Cop process but as “a successful defence of the [UN climate convention’s] integrity against a coordinated attack by a few countries implacably opposed to action on climate change, in particular to any mention of the need to transition away from fossil fuels”.

Amanda Cahill, founder of the Next Economy, was in Antalya to offer advice on elements of the conference dealing with the so-called “just transition” – a wide-reaching set of guidelines meant to protect communities and workers affected by climate change and the shift away from the fossil fuel industry.

“While we didn’t get the outcome we wanted at this Cop, we maintained the global commitment to justice and equity as countries transition their economies to deal with climate change,” she said.

“We’ve got a lot of work ahead of us, but parties have committed to ensuring the Just Transition Mechanism is set up and that countries can get the support they need to implement meaningful and just climate action.”

Adam Bandt, the former Greens leader and chief executive of the Australian Conservation Foundation, said countries had “understandably” rejected a pact that he said “failed to even mention the main causes of the climate crisis, let alone address them”.

“The prime minister’s snub of the UN secretary general by failing to mention coal and gas in his speech set the tone early in this summit,” he said.

items.body:
Jim Chalmers has told parliament the mid-year economic and fiscal outlook will include ‘net savings’ to assist in the ongoing battle against persistently high price pressures. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP

Jim Chalmers has told parliament the mid-year economic and fiscal outlook will include ‘net savings’ to assist in the ongoing battle against persistently high price pressures. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP

Unemployment to surpass 5% and ‘things will get a bit harder’, treasurer Jim Chalmers warns

Economists flag rising recession risk as government forecasts economy will grow by less than 2% in 2027 and 2028

• Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updates

• Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

Jim Chalmers has warned Australians that “things will get a bit harder before they get easier”, revealing next month’s budget update will show unemployment climbing above 5% alongside slower economic growth for the next two years.

As economists flagged rising recessionary risks, the treasurer used a ministerial statement during question time to reveal what he described as “concerning” economic numbers in the upcoming mid-year economic and fiscal outlook.

Alongside higher unemployment, high fuel costs meant inflation would slow from 4.7% now to only “the mid-3s” by the middle of next year – or about 1 percentage point higher than anticipated in the May budget.

The economy was now expected to grow by less than 2% in both 2027 and 2028.

“We say with humility and with honesty that things might get a bit harder before they get easier,” Chalmers told parliament.

Five fights Labor wants to win before the end of the parliamentary year

Read more

“If Treasury was updating the mid-year forecasts today, they would reflect this difficult environment we’re in. In the near term, they’d forecast softer growth, higher inflation and higher unemployment.”

With a majority of Australians blaming public spending for driving this year’s inflation outbreak, Chalmers promised that the mid-year economic and fiscal outlook will include “net savings” to assist in the ongoing battle against persistently high price pressures.

• Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

“It’s not a mini-budget full of new initiatives but it will have some budget-sized savings. At this stage, we expect to more than offset our new spending decisions, without slashing and burning the services people rely on,” he said.

News last week that the unemployment rate had climbed to 4.9% in October has turbocharged fears that a series of Reserve Bank interest rate hikes are weighing more heavily than anticipated – and that the economy could even tip into a deeper downturn next year.

Chalmers said the government’s short-term goal was “cutting spending enough, without threatening growth” – an approach he described as “a delicate balance”.

“We know that no realistic amount of savings makes inflation go away, but too much new spending can make it worse,” he said.

With the full effect of the five rate hikes only likely to become apparent through 2027, Shane Oliver, AMP’s chief economist, predicted economic growth would slump from 2.3%, to below 1%.

skip past newsletter promotion

after newsletter promotion

“We could flirt with recession next year,” Oliver said, putting the chances of a more severe downturn at a “high and rising” 40%.

Official figures on Wednesday are likely to show inflation climbing to nearly 5%, and Oliver agreed with the treasurer that getting the settings right in the mid-year budget would be “a difficult balancing act”.

“The government has been copping political blame for inflation, and Chalmers is under a lot of pressure to cut [spending]; but if he cuts too much it could accentuate the recession risks.”

The treasurer foreshadowed that any new spending decisions – such as Monday’s announcement that the $25 price cap on prescription medicine would be extended until the end of the decade at a cost of $242m – would be more than offset by savings measures.

But he also flagged that the mix of a weaker economy and “big unavoidable spending commitments” meant bigger deficits in the later years of the forward estimates period.

“It would not be responsible to fully offset these big changes to revenue and payments that flow through automatically from weaker economic parameters,” he argued.

With the full effect of the five rate hikes only likely to become apparent through 2027, Shane Oliver, AMP’s chief economist, predicted economic growth would slump from 2.3%, to below 1%.

“We could flirt with recession next year,” Oliver said, putting the chances of a more severe downturn at a “high and rising” 40%.

A joint coronial inquest in Lismore has heard that three babies died after being born in free births, and a fourth during a home birth between 2022 and 2024. Photograph: AAP

A joint coronial inquest in Lismore has heard that three babies died after being born in free births, and a fourth during a home birth between 2022 and 2024. Photograph: AAP

Doula thought self-described birth keeper was clinically trained before NSW baby death, inquest hears

Inquest into the deaths of four babies after free and home births hears doula urged client to attend birth centre

• Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updates

• Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A doula who supported a free birth without any medical professionals present has told an inquest that she thought a self-described birth keeper who was assisting her was clinically trained.

The child, known in court as Baby R, died after the free birth. Baby R’s death is one of four being examined in a joint coronial inquest in Lismore, which has heard that three babies died after being born in free births, and a fourth during a home birth between 2022 and 2024.

Sita Tara Kali, a doula who was expected to give evidence later on Monday, was involved in the care of two of the four babies – including Baby R, who is thought to have died of “severe post-maturity” after being born at 43 weeks and one day in a free birth.

On Monday morning, another doula present for Baby R’s birth, Ione Maslin, gave evidence at the inquest.

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email

Maslin told the inquest that she was not medically trained, and had attended about 30 to 40 births before Baby R’s death. She said that Baby R’s birth was the first she had attended without a midwife present.

She told the inquest she now wouldn’t feel comfortable supporting a birth without a midwife present because “doulas need to be working together with the healthcare system”.

Mother whose twin baby died was determined to have home birth despite advice of experts, NSW inquest hears

Read more

The inquest heard that the baby’s mother had hoped that the Byron Bay Birth Centre would be able to provide her with a midwife, but that the she was told she lived too far away.

“She started looking for a private midwife but still she maintained the hope that the hospital would be able to provide her with care,” Maslin, who is from Brazil, told the inquest through a Portuguese translator.

“I insisted for her to go to the birth centre to have the baby … I suggested her to go and visit and feel the energy and to know that it was OK and safe.”

The inquest last week heard that Baby R’s mother had a general distrust of hospitals and felt that having a home birth would give her a stronger connection to her baby.

Maslin told the inquest that Kali had come on as a second doula during the pregnancy. She said she was under the impression that Kali was clinically trained, but was “not a registered professional”.

skip past newsletter promotion

after newsletter promotion

Self-described birth keeper Sita Tara Kali, also known as Mumma Sita. Photograph: GoFundMe

The inquest last week heard that, at 43 weeks, an ultrasound confirmed that Baby R was extremely compromised. The obstetric advice was urgent, and the mother was urged to attend emergency and strongly advised against a home birth.

The woman contacted Kali, the inquest heard, who said in a police statement that “she was quite upset and anxious. I advised her to go home and rest. ‘Calm yourself down and consider what you want to do’.”

Baby R was born outside into his father’s hands at 9.51am. He was white in colour and never latched on to feed, the inquest heard.

About 14 hours later, the ambulance was called. The umbilical cord and placenta were still attached. Baby R died on the way to a waiting helicopter at 12.22am.

The court heard that Baby R likely died of “severe post-maturity” after being born at 43 weeks and one day. The standard is to induce birth or perform a caesarean section at 42 weeks, as the ageing placenta puts the baby at risk.

The inquest continues.

items.summary: Scientific and satellite findings warn of widespread contamination in Gaza, posing grave threats to public health ‘for generations to come’ Israel’s destruction of Gaza has left a devastating environmental legacy with poisoned water, contaminated soil and toxic air threatening the life-support syste…
items.body:
Palestinians among the wreckage of shelters after demolition operations carried out by the Israeli army near Al-Maghazi refugee camp last week. Photograph: Ahmed Ibrahim/APAImages/Shutterstock

Palestinians among the wreckage of shelters after demolition operations carried out by the Israeli army near Al-Maghazi refugee camp last week. Photograph: Ahmed Ibrahim/APAImages/Shutterstock

Israel’s destruction of Gaza has created a ‘toxic wasteland’, experts find

Scientific and satellite findings warn of widespread contamination in Gaza, posing grave threats to public health ‘for generations to come’

Israel’s destruction of Gaza has left a devastating environmental legacy with poisoned water, contaminated soil and toxic air threatening the life-support systems that the population depends on for survival, according to a report.

Israel’s military assault has created widespread contamination across the entire strip, the report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (Ceobs) finds, with heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and sewage making the air, soil and water dangerous for Palestinians for decades to come.

Oxfam International’s executive director, Amitabh Behar, said: “Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come.”

He said the “destruction and contamination of Gaza” have “fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival” and breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law.

“Palestinians living in Gaza are being exposed to toxins … through air, food, water and via direct contact with contaminated soils and debris. These risks will persist for generations to come, unless clean-up, remediation and recovery actions are prioritised.”

Land bulldozed by Israeli forces near the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza last week. Photograph: Omar Ashtawy/HL/Getty

In 2025 and earlier this year, the UN independent international commission of inquiry found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and that Israeli officials, including the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, incited these acts. The Israeli mission in Geneva said Israel rejected the commission’s “libellous sham”. Netanyahu is separately wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) for war crimes.

Oxfam’s report gives the most comprehensive picture to date of what it calls the “toxic wasteland” created by the Israeli assault which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded at least 175,000, while thousands still remain unaccounted for under the rubble.

Using satellite imagery, remote sensing, scientific analysis and other open-source data, it concludes contamination in Gaza is “widespread, severe and consequential, with serious implications for public health and civilian survival”.

Behar said: “It is horrifying to begin to understand the extent of toxic contamination being faced by the population, who can neither escape nor protect themselves properly from the dangers. In an area as small, oppressed and densely populated as Gaza, continuous exposure is inevitable, with people surrounded by waste and sewage, spreading pests and the risk of disease growing.

“Raw sewage is pouring into the sea and leaking into the ground, while the destruction of Gaza’s sanitation systems leaves people with little protection from the contamination around them.”

Displaced Palestinians living near a rubbish-filled sewage waste flow in Gaza City. The destruction of sanitation systems leaves people with little protection from contamination. Photograph: Ahmad Hasaballah/Getty

He added the “associated health consequences will be severe, with children and pregnant women among those facing the highest risks”.

The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimates that Israel’s military operations have generated more than 61m tonnes of debris across the territory, turning Gaza’s destroyed homes, neighbourhoods and infrastructure into a vast reservoir of potentially hazardous materials.

The report’s author, Lama Abdul Samad, a global water and sanitation specialist at Oxfam, said tackling the environmental damage in Gaza will be “highly challenging because contamination is dispersed across the urban rubble, farmland, water systems and soils, while unexploded ordnance continues to restrict safe access to most areas”.

Children walk past an unexploded missile at a Gaza City rubbish dump. Photograph: Majdi Fathi/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

“The analysis highlights the urgent need for Israel to grant access for a detailed environmental assessment on the ground to clarify the risks to public health and identify options for urgent harm-reduction measures. Restoration is likely to require extensive clearance, monitoring and specialised remediation of affected areas from contaminants such as explosive residues, organic pollutants and heavy metals.”

Behar said that as international attention increasingly turned to Gaza’s reconstruction, environmental recovery must not be treated as an afterthought, but as a vital undertaking in parallel.

“Rebuilding Gaza without simultaneously understanding and addressing the extent of environmental contamination risks creating long-term public health consequences for generations to come,” he said.

The Israeli government has been contacted for comment.

items.body:
Authorities respond after concertgoers were evacuated from the US rapper Don Toliver’s Manchester show after reports of gas being released into the crowd. Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images

Authorities respond after concertgoers were evacuated from the US rapper Don Toliver’s Manchester show after reports of gas being released into the crowd. Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images

Manchester’s Co-op Live arena evacuated after apparent tear gas incident at Don Toliver concert

Incident occurred near the end of Sunday night show by US rapper Don Toliver, with one person taken to hospital

Police have evacuated Manchester’s Co-op Live arena after a substance believed to be teargas was let off in the crowd during a Don Toliver concert.

Greater Manchester police said the incident occurred near the end of the US rapper’s show on Sunday evening.

Greater Manchester police said concertgoers had been safely evacuated, with several people being assessed on site for side effects as a precaution and inquiries under way to determine what the substance was. No serious injuries have been reported.

Assistant chief constable Steph Parker said in a statement: “Our priority was to ensure the safety of every person that was attending the concert.

“Several people were treated on site, and one has been taken to hospital at this time. Anyone who has left the event and since become unwell is advised to attend their local hospital.

“We understand the concern that this incident will have raised – particularly those with loved ones at the venue last night – and we’d like to thank everyone for their patience as we dealt with it.

“There were over 12,000 people in attendance during this concert who were safely escorted from the arena so they could make their way home.”

She continued: “Our declaration of a major incident has allowed us to ensure emergency services and partner agencies can work together quickly and effectively to coordinate a safe response.

“We will now begin to fully understand what this substance was and how this incident came about.”

The north-west ambulance service said one person was taken to hospital and more than 50 were assessed by clinicians.

The service said in a statement: “We deployed several emergency crews, including our Hazardous Area Response Team, to support the safe assessment and treatment of people at the scene.

“More than 50 people have been assessed by our clinicians, with some reporting eye and respiratory symptoms. Decontamination is being carried out as a precaution and one patient has been taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment.

“The incident remains ongoing and our teams remain at the scene assessing and caring for patients. We continue to work closely with emergency service partners while inquiries are carried out to establish what the substance was.

“Anyone at tonight’s event who has since noticed side effects or become ill should seek medical advice.”

Footage shared on social media appeared to show concertgoers coughing and covering their mouths as they left the venue.

Co-op Live has the capacity to hold 23,500 people, with American singer Phoebe Bridgers scheduled to perform at the venue on Thursday.

Don Toliver is partway through the UK leg of his Octane World Tour.

items.title: Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
items.summary: Libya's eastern government says the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia.
items.body:
Image source, Planet Labs PBC

Image caption,

Satellite imagery showed a ship on fire early on Sunday morning

ByHafsa Khalil

Updated 4 minutes ago

An explosion has occurred on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port after a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.

The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libyan state media reported, citing the eastern government.

It added that the site was secured, and there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.

Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC, reviewed by BBC Verify, shows a boat on fire at 0547 GMT at the Benghazi port, with a separate image captured several hours later appearing to show the same vessel partially submerged.

Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship engulfed in flames and smoke, while it is still dark.

The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.

Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.

GNS said the country was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.

Seperately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.

GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".

Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.

items.summary: Footage of Saturday incident, filmed by fellow passengers, quickly went viral on social media as mayor calls tactics ‘un-American’ Protesters marched through the Seattle-Tacoma international airport on Sunday after widely shared footage captured masked immigration agents detaining a father and daugh…
items.body:
The moment an ICE agent detains a father and daughter boarding flight at Seattle airport - video

Video of ICE detaining father and daughter while boarding flight sparks protests in Seattle

Footage of Saturday incident, filmed by fellow passengers, quickly went viral on social media as mayor calls tactics ‘un-American’

Protesters marched through the Seattle-Tacoma international airport on Sunday after widely shared footage captured masked immigration agents detaining a father and daughter on an airport jet bridge as they boarded their Alaska Airlines flight.

Video of the incident on Saturday – filmed by fellow passengers – quickly went viral on social media, sparking condemnation from lawmakers, including Washington Democratic governor Bob Ferguson and Seattle mayor Katie Wilson.

Footage and photographs showed protesters with bullhorns and signs that read “ICE out of Washington” and “Abolish ICE” at the Seattle airport. Protesters could be seen walking inside and around the airport chanting “ICE out now” and other rallying cries.

They went out to celebrate at a Memphis bar. Then, ICE descended

Read more

“I made my view very clear to Alaska Airlines: They need to call on ICE to get out of our airports,” Ferguson said in a briefing. “I’ll be making that request of every other airline that operates at SeaTac airport as well.”

On Sunday a lawyer representing Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza and his daughter, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, said they were heading to a family baptism ceremony in California when they were detained by masked agents.

Protesters at the Seattle airport after US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers arrested two people boarding an Alaska Airlines flight. Photograph: David Ryder/Reuters

Other passengers boarding the Alaska Airlines flight at Seattle-Tacoma international airport used their cellphones to film the father and daughter being detained by the officers, who were wearing unmarked jackets and khaki pants.

The videos show the officers struggling with someone on the ground. The flight, bound for Los Angeles, was delayed.

ICE has stepped up operations at airports since the summer as the agency has shifted tactics from sweeping urban raids to more targeted operations in all corners of US, with arrests reaching record levels.

Ferguson called ICE’s tactics “deeply un-American” and called for the agency’s abolition.

“The video is horrific and it is chilling,” Ferguson said at a news conference on Saturday with labor leaders and local elected officials.

Wilson called ICE’s tactics “unacceptable and un-American”.

In a statement to the Guardian, ICE said its officers detained Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico, who it said had overstayed his visa “in violation of our nation’s laws”.

items.title: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
items.summary: Democrats have now won at least 258 seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats.
items.body:
Image source, Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images

Image caption,

Chuck Hubbard is a former journalist whose first political campaign was in 2022

ByMadeline Halpert

The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.

The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.

The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.

Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.

• View the 2026 midterm election results

Sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.

She conceded on Sunday, saying in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."

Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images

Image caption,

Virginia Foxx spent a decade in the North Carolina Senate before representing the state in the House of Representatives

Hubbard, meanwhile, wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".

He added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."

Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx in the 2024 midterms by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa.

Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters.

President Donald Trump himself has suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses, as well as Vice President JD Vance.

Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website.

The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes.

Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law.

However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation.

items.title: US army to blow up bomb-making chemicals despite safety concerns
items.summary: Army invokes emergency provisions in Iowa to avoid court order despite worries about health and environment risks The US army plans to invoke emergency provisions to avoid a court order that had put on hold plans to detonate several tons of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa , saying that continued delay…
items.body:
Residential buildings stand near the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant as residents make plans for the US army's detonation of a degraded stockpile of lead azide in Middletown, Iowa. Photograph: Jim Urquhart/Reuters

Residential buildings stand near the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant as residents make plans for the US army's detonation of a degraded stockpile of lead azide in Middletown, Iowa. Photograph: Jim Urquhart/Reuters

US army to blow up bomb-making chemicals despite safety concerns

Army invokes emergency provisions in Iowa to avoid court order despite worries about health and environment risks

The US army plans to invoke emergency provisions to avoid a court order that had put on hold plans to detonate several tons of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa, saying that continued delays will make it more dangerous as the weather starts to turn colder.

“To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action,” government lawyers told the eight US circuit court of appeals in a filing late on Saturday. “Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay.”

The army plans to detonate the chemicals by Tuesday.

Environmental groups criticized the government’s move, decrying it as a maneuver to get around a court order and avoid public demands for safety and transparency.

The appeals court on Thursday granted a request by environmentalists to put on hold a permit that cleared the way for the detonation in Middletown, a small community about 160 miles (257km) south-east of Des Moines. It was initially planned for Friday, but the army later announced that it would push the operation to Monday after an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects.

US army postpones plan to detonate bomb-making chemical amid outcry

Read more

Environmentalists have called for a review of the emergency permit that was approved earlier this month by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

In a statement on Sunday, the Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club and Earthjustice questioned claims that all alternatives were given appropriate consideration.

“The Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public’s demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm,” said Thien Chau, an attorney at Earthjustice.

Government lawyers said the army doesn’t need a permit to take emergency action against an immediate threat from explosive material.

They said the standards of a federal law regulating hazardous waste don’t apply in situations when there is an immediate threat to health, safety or the environment as determined by an explosive or munitions emergency response specialist.

Officials contend that the chemicals are unstable, and the risk of an uncontrolled explosion is growing, particularly as temperatures drop. They said there is a risk that the chemicals may explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30F (-1C) in the coming days.

In March, staff at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant found several dozen barrels of degraded lead azide, which is used in munitions production. Crystallization of the material created an unstable and dangerous situation, prompting the army to assemble experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with a plan.

According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the drums’ contents with other chemicals were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal detonation.

The environmental groups disagreed, arguing in their petition that other alternatives were not fully considered. They also criticized officials for not sharing more information with the public.

Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, but thousands more in surrounding areas could be affected by detonated material that could disperse in the air and land on the ground.

Iowans in the region were told to stay inside, keep windows and doors closed, bring pets and livestock indoors, and clean cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces after.

“The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground,” an advisory states. “Lead is toxic to humans and animals.”

items.title: COP31 fails to reach major climate deal as talks expose deep divisions
items.summary: Hopes for an agreement on tackling climate change collapsed after a row about mentioning fossil fuels
items.body:
Image source, Reuters

ByMark Poynting, Esme Stallard and Justin Rowlatt

BBC Climate and Science

Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.

Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.

But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.

Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.

The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.

UN secretary general Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".

He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".

After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday morning to try to break the deadlock.

But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023, when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.

The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change".

"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.

Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.

A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.

Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions.

Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too quickly it would lead to "fuel poverty".

Figure caption,

What’s next after no deal at COP31 climate talks?

Another major sticking point has been money for poorer countries to adapt to the impacts of climate change, such as more intense heatwaves and more severe droughts.

Last year at COP30 in Brazil, nations agreed to triple the finance for that purpose.

But this year's deal contained no reference to concrete figures, nor the baseline against which that pledge would be measured. This raised fears it would give richer nations too much wriggle room.

"Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed," said Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, an African climate and energy think tank.

The UK's Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, described the failure to reach a political agreement as "immensely disappointing".

"This only strengthens our resolve to work with partners around the world on the genuine progress made in Antalya on tackling the climate crisis," she said, adding that the UK's commitment was "unwavering".

Climate talks in an age of 'overshoot'

While talks were hosted in Antalya in Turkey, Australia led the official negotiations - creating what some observers described as a chaotic dynamic.

Chris Bowen, Australian government minister and COP31 president of negotiations, said that there were "unbridgeable red lines" in the discussions.

He pointed to "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". At the same time, "the impacts of climate change are getting worse", he said, raising the stakes.

The year 2026 could end as the hottest on record and has brought extreme weather and natural hazards to much of the world, from summer heat and drought in Europe to flash flooding in Nepal.

And COP31 was the first annual UN conference to formally discuss how one of the key international targets for limiting climate change would be missed.

In the Paris talks of 2015, nearly 200 countries agreed to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels of the late 1800s, aimed at avoiding some of the worst effects of climate change.

The UN says that the Paris deal has driven "near-universal" climate action. In the early 2010s, global warming of 4C or more was thought to be a serious possibility by the end of the century.

Now, the world is likely to limit warming to about 2.8C by 2100 based on current government policies, the UN says.

But action has not been fast enough to meet that Paris goal, with the world likely to "overshoot" 1.5C of long-term warming in the next few years.

Many countries say they are committed to eventually bringing warming back down to 1.5C, but that will require an ambitious ramping up of technologies - which do not yet exist at scale - to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

Although the main deal fell through, some agreements were reached, including progress on a "just transition mechanism" - a framework to support workers and communities as economies shift towards clean energy.

The COP31 president also said that more than 80 countries backed Turkey's target to increase the share of global energy use met by electricity to 35% by 2035

But following today's events, some have questioned whether the UN climate process - which relies on consensus - can succeed in a geopolitically divided world.

The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the process, with the next conference scheduled for November 2027, COP32 in Ethiopia.

"[The consensus process] has worked to get us where we are," he told the BBC. "It got us through Paris... so it can work," but acknowledged it "fell short" today.

The UN climate process has "suffered setback before and come back stronger," Stiell told delegates. "It must do so again."

But following today's events, some have questioned whether the UN climate process - which relies on consensus - can succeed in a geopolitically divided world.

items.title: Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
items.summary: In a statement to Italian media, his family remember him as "the greatest jeweller of our time".
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

ByJessica Lamb

Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.

His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media.

Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales.

The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".

The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.

Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.

Paolo Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.

Image source, Reuters

The Bulgari family favoured bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected colour combinations to set them apart from the delicate asethetic associated with Parisian jewellery houses.

The business broke into luxury markets and diversified beyond jewellery into watches, perfumes, leather goods and hotels.

"Paolo Bulgari began collaborating with his father in 1960, specialising in the knowledge of precious stones, of which he was one of the world's leading experts, and refining the sensibility and aesthetic sense that are at the root of the Bvlgari style," the Bvlgari company posted on social media., external

"He poured his heart into his craft and into nurturing the talents of young designers, leaving an indelible mark on the world of jewellery.

"Thank you, Mr. Paolo, your legacy as a brilliant beacon of creative inspiration will continue to inspire generations to come."

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Paolo Bulgari alongside David Bowie and his wife Iman in September 1991 in Versailles, France.

The post included a quote from Paolo Bulgari: "Everything can be a source of inspiration. There are no rules in creativity. Never."

The designer brand's celebrity clients have included Elizabeth Taylor, Audrey Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe, Ingrid Bergman, Sophie Loren, Anne Hathaway, Zendaya and Rihanna.

Image source, FilmMagic via Getty Images

Image caption,

Actor Zendaya wearing a Bvlgari necklace at the 2025 Golden Globe awards.

In 2011 the family sold its controlling stake to the French luxury group LVMH, in a deal worth about 3.7 billion euros.

In 2019, he and his wife established the Paolo Bulgari Foundation to support young people through schooling and job training in disadvantaged neighbourhoods on the outskirts of Rome.

The funeral will take place in Rome on Monday, 23 November in the Basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.

items.body:
Donald Trump gestures to reporters while taking questions during a news briefing in the White House on Friday in Washington DC. Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

Donald Trump gestures to reporters while taking questions during a news briefing in the White House on Friday in Washington DC. Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

Trump hosts third crypto gala for meme coin amid conflict of interest outcry

Virginia dinner comes as Democrats accuse president of improperly profiting from his cryptocurrency ventures

Donald Trump is scheduled to headline his third cryptocurrency gala on ⁠Sunday night at his ​country club in Virginia, rewarding top holders of his own meme coin as Democrats accuse the president of improperly profiting from his crypto ventures.

The dinner, set to take place at the Trump National Golf Club in Sterling, Virginia, will include meet-and-greets with Trump supporters including the boxing champion Floyd Mayweather, Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary, NBA champion Tristan Thompson and mentalist Lior Suchard, according to the event’s website.

The gala’s access and perks are divided by tiers for the 185 holders of $TRUMP, the president’s meme coin. A Trump fragrance, a poster, a “commemorative” ticket, and a “Trump watch” are reserved for 120 attendees. Meanwhile, the top 29 investors are invited to a VIP reception, and the top four will receive a “TRUMP 18K Gold Watch”.

Trump has hosted two similar galas since he took office last year, bringing a flurry of criticism as Democrats accuse Trump and his family of monetizing his brand through an array of equities and crypto ventures while in office.

A statue of Donald Trump holding a bitcoin in recognition of his support for cryptocurrency is displayed on the National Mall in September 2025 in Washington DC. Photograph: Alex Brandon/AP

After sweepingwins in the midterms, Democrats have vowed to investigate conflicts of interest involving Trump and his personal wealth during his presidency. They also say they plan to push for legislation that would ban activities such as the meme coin gala dinner.

“This dinner and scoring mechanism appear carefully constructed to increase investment in $TRUMP, allowing the President to abuse the power of his office to personally enrich himself, as he has throughout this term,” reads a letter sent by Adam Schiff and eight other US senators last month.

Since returning to the White House, Trump has made more than $1bn from his crypto businesses, according to financial disclosures released in June. Trump received more than $500m from his World Liberty Financial business selling new crypto products, and raked another $600m from sales of souvenir-type “meme” coins stamped with Trump’s face. Trump launched his $Trump meme coin days before his inauguration.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Interest in the $TRUMP coin dinner has plummeted, with contestants’ combined holdings dropping from $148m in May 2025 to $8.6m in this month’s gala.

More than half of the digital wallets publicly listed on the contest leaderboard for Sunday’s dinner are tied directly to crypto exchanges that bar US-based users, indicating they ‌are linked to foreign nationals, according to an analysis of blockchain data prepared for Reuters by the nonpartisan, non-profit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen.

Demonstrators hold up mock cryptocurrency during a rally Against Trump's crypto dealings at the Trump National Golf Club in May 2025 in Virginia. Photograph: Jemal Countess/Getty Images for Public Citizen

“Neither the President nor his family ⁠has ever engaged — or will ever engage — in conflicts of interest,” White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Reuters ​earlier this year. “President Trump proudly made ​the United States the crypto capital of the world ​through executive actions.“

The Trump family’s other crypto-connected equities and ventures have also fallen in value to record ​lows. Together, outside investors in their ‌five main crypto and ​crypto-linked projects have lost more than $5bn​, according to a Reuters analysis.

The Trump meme coin has earned the Trump family at least $635m, according to the president’s June financial disclosure statement. In total, the Trumps had earned at least $2.3bn through April from their four main crypto ventures, including the meme coin.

The president’s stake in a fifth crypto-linked venture, Trump Media & Technology Group, is worth about $430m.

Reuters contributed reporting

items.title: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
items.summary: AI employees in the industry's epicentre - San Francisco - worry that the sector is overheated.
items.body:
Image source, San Francisco Travel Association

Image caption,

The city of San Francisco is the heart of the AI sector

ByZoe Corbyn

Technology reporter, Reporting fromSan Francisco

Lauren Goldboss is busy. The owner of a small San Francisco dog-walking company, she has been hiring staff and buying vans.

Fuelling the growth is her new office dog-walking service Paw Perk, popular with some local AI start-ups.

Her business is an example of how the AI boom in San Francisco is benefiting other sectors.

The city saw an exodus of residents during the pandemic and its downtown was weakened by remote work, but it s now enjoying a rejuvenation, with AI being the major driver.

Image source, Lauren Goldboss

Image caption,

Lauren Goldboss walks dogs for AI workers

Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.

Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up, external in San Francisco.

Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.

But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn, external that this was a possibility.

Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (£49bn).

• Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?Published4 days ago

• The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandalPublished12 November

• Wealthy AI workers send San Francisco house prices soaringPublished9 July

• Follow the money: Who pays for the AI boom now?

What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco – no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles – be preparing for a possible crash?

One AI worker, employed by one of the largest companies in the city, is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come down… and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.

He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.

But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"

Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".

Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.

"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."

If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.

That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.

One study, external found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.

But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.

For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.

"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.

Ted Egan, the chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, adds that "because of AI, it is a good time for tech again in the city, but we are not seeing tonnes of overall tech job growth".

Despite the expansion of the AI sector, the city remains about 35,000 jobs shy of its pre-pandemic peak, estimates Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley.

Instead, much of the spending by AI firms in the US is going towards data centres and computing power, relatively little of which are located in the Bay Area. San Francisco might be the brains of the AI boom, but it isn't the brawn.

Nonetheless, a significant correction could still be "very painful" for San Francisco, warns Moretti. Less AI hiring and potential layoffs would ripple through the local service sector, likely to affect jobs in everything from restaurants, to retail, to personal services like dog walking.

"It is the spillover on service jobs that would actually be the main effect," he says.

Office vacancies could also rise, reducing downtown foot traffic, while rents and house prices could weaken.

Image caption,

Huge data centres are being built across the US to power AI

But AI isn't the only force driving San Francisco's recovery. Healthcare and tourism – which the city has been working to encourage, including by improving downtown safety and cleanliness – are also growing,, external which may help cushion against a possible AI downturn.

"Tourism is not fully back, but the growth has been healthy," says Egan, adding that it is a sign of confidence in San Francisco.

All told, Egan doesn't expect an AI crash to fundamentally alter San Francisco's economic trajectory.

"The city's economy has not been screaming during this AI boom, so I wouldn't expect it to grind to a halt if there was a slowdown in AI spending," he says. "I think of it primarily as a hiccup that we should expect, rather than a major course correction for the city's economy."

As to whether and how San Francisco's city government should prepare, there are limits to what it can do, note Bellisario and Moretti. But encouraging growth in sectors beyond technology and maintaining financial reserves could help.

For Goldboss, the dog-walking company owner, her philosophy is to "build while it is here". If the next tech bust comes – "always a reality in San Francisco" – she will try to adapt to what the market needs. "It is just the risk you kind of have to take," she says.

items.title: Burnham to tell MPs 'landmark' EU deal could make next decade 'much better'
items.summary: The prime minister will tell MPs the deal agreed on Friday is a "choice between a broken status quo or change".
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Andy Burnham agreed a deal with the EU in Brussels on Friday

ByNick Eardley, Political correspondent and Matt Spivey

The prime minister will tell Parliament on Monday the "landmark" deal struck with the EU means there is a "very real prospect" the next decade can be "much better" than the last one.

The deal is a "choice between a broken status quo or change", Andy Burnham will tell MPs.

He will also call it "the single biggest growth measure to be delivered in this parliament" - repeating his claim it could add £17bn to the British economy.

The PM described it on Friday as a "win-win" deal with the EU on British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. But since then a host of politicians have criticised the plan, with one former prime minister urging him to "move on" from Brexit.

Burnham believes the agreement reached in Brussels "holds out the very real prospect that the next decade can be a much better one for Britain than the one we have just lived through".

"The ability to draw a line on a decade of drift and division is in our hands and I believe we should take it," he will say in his speech.

He will also paint the move as a choice "between easing pressure on the cost of living or allowing food prices to rise further" and "creating opportunities for young people or denying them".

He believes polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

But his announcement on Friday was greeted with a chorus of criticism from a number of opposing political figures.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal was unfair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels.

She questioned the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".

Badenoch accused him of having "plucked that figure out of the air" before saying "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".

Meanwhile Reform UK leader Farage called the deal a "very good day for the EU", before adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."

Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added in a social media post: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."

Over the weekend former prime ministers including Theresa May, Sir Tony Blair and Rishi Sunak also criticised the EU-UK deal.

May, who presided over three years of Brexit negotiations during her premiership, said she was "aghast" by the deal and warned Andy Burnham should "move on".

'Danger seems greater all the time': Ukrainians search for missing after Russian strikes

'Danger seems greater all the time': Ukrainians search for missing after Russian strikes

At least three bodies have been recovered the site of a residential building that was hit by a Russian strike in the Kyiv region, Ukraine's State Emergency Services said.

A woman in her forties and a teenage boy have so far been identified as rescue workers continue to search the rubble for those who are still trapped.

Continued warnings of further drone threats near the site are hampering efforts, the service added, but some people were successfully evacuated earlier in the day.

"We are living a nightmare... only God knows when it will end," one woman told the BBC's Sarah Rainsford, who's reporting from Ukraine's Kyiv region.

items.body:
Abdul El-Sayed speaks about the Democrats’ historic midterm success and his priorities as a senator during the Atlantic’s summit in Washington DC on 17 November. Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/Reuters

Abdul El-Sayed speaks about the Democrats’ historic midterm success and his priorities as a senator during the Atlantic’s summit in Washington DC on 17 November. Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/Reuters

Abdul El-Sayed doubles down on ‘TrumpCare’ health plan, urging president to ‘get it done’

Democratic senator-elect reiterates suggestion to rename Medicare for All after Trump if president allows bill to pass

Michigan US senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday doubled down on naming healthcare reform legislation after Donald Trump as long as it meant the president would not impede its passage.

“If he’s open to the conversation, I am open to it, too,” El-Sayed said of Trump on Sunday. “If the president is opening to signing that bill, let’s get it done.”

El-Sayed made those remarks on Sunday on NBC’s Meet the Press, where he reiterated his pledge to pursue a single-payer, national healthcare program after the Democrat became the first Muslim person elected to the US Senate during the midterms earlier in November.

‘I agree with the president’: incoming senator Abdul El-Sayed seeks to help Trump end military aid to Israel

Read more

Trump’s Republican party is going to lose control of Congress for the second half of his second presidency. But the president has made clear his intention to wield his legislative veto powers whenever he sees fit.

Appearing on Sunday’s Meet the Press, El-Sayed said he would not mind Medicare for All – a big part of his campaign platform – being named “TrumpCare” as long as such a program came into existence.

“I care that the people of this country finally have the unmet promise of guaranteed healthcare in this country. And if the president is serious about leaving a lasting legacy, there is nothing better than the ultimate Trump card,” El-Sayed said to Meet the Press host Kristen Welker, making a double entendre for a term that – when the T is lowercase – also refers to a card that beats out others in card games.

El-Sayed told Welker that such a Trump card would be in effect “from the moment [people] are born to the moment that they pass away – that guarantees them the healthcare that has been so elusive in this country without premiums, co-pays and deductibles”.

The senator-elect’s comments come after he previously suggested to CNN that he is not above stroking Trump’s prodigious ego to get legislation passed – including by naming Medicare for All “TrumpCare”.

He also previously wrote on social media, alongside images of a gold health insurance card with “TrumpCare” inscribed on it: “Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”

Trump has spent much of his second presidency trying to get as much as possible named after him – from institutions, physical buildings and currency.

El-Sayed also said that he supports healthcare reform proposed by Bernie Sanders, the progressive US senator.

‘A complete repudiation’: public health won big in US midterm elections

Read more

Sanders’ proposal would create a single-payer system in which the federal government insures everybody, financed by an increase in taxes, while eliminating private insurance.

But El-Sayed said he is not focused on eliminating private insurance as an option, which Sanders aims to eliminate by having everything primary and preventive services to hospital stays covered under his proposed plan. Out-of-pocket costs on deductibles and co-pays – staples of the rapacious private insurance industry to which most Americans must resort – would also be eliminated under Sanders’ plan.

El-Sayed said he wants to “provide you basic public health insurance no matter who you are in this country” while being open to the idea of not taking alternative options away.

The senator-elect said he has a meeting on the books with JD Vance. El-Sayed would not share the agenda of the meeting, but he confirmed that the vice-president’s chief of staff contacted him after his election victory.

Theresa May might not like the idea of revisiting Brexit but did not even try to argue that it had been a success. Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/Shutterstock

Analysis

Theresa May’s blast from the past calls Tories back to their unhappy place

Peter Walker

Conservatives may instinctively want to push back against closer EU ties, but they have to train their focus elsewhere

Anyone who accidentally switched to BBC One at about 9.45am on Sunday to be greeted by Theresa May awkwardly espousing the virtues of Brexit could have been forgiven for thinking they had woken up in around 2018 – and not being especially pleased at the idea.

This is one of the problems now facing May’s party. For all that it is a reflex action for Conservatives to push back against closer ties with the EU, Andy Burnham’s decision to pursue such a course plunges them back into their own unhappy place.

For Tory MPs and activists with a full set of Brexit campaign medals, this risks being especially triggering. May’s repeated attempts to cobble together a departure deal that could unite her party involved repeated humiliations, among them the heaviest ever parliamentary defeat for a British PM, when the Commons rejected her Brexit plan by a majority of 230.

With the afterglow of Boris Johnson’s “get Brexit done” 2019 election triumph now seven years and four prime ministers ago, under Kemi Badenoch the party has opted to do less of the, in David Cameron’s resonant phrase, “banging on about Europe” and instead focus on policy areas such as the economy, social security and defence.

The reasons for this caution are obvious. To begin with, even more ardent Tory Brexiters struggle to articulate any tangible benefits to the UK in the decade since the referendum, beyond slightly niche constitutional points about self-determination.

In her BBC interview, May, who comments sparingly on live political subjects despite being an active Tory peer, did not even try to argue that Brexit had been a success, instead saying it was impossible to know, given events such as Covid and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and then adding: “I don’t think Britain’s state today is about whether or not we left the European Union.”

Many voters are much clearer about what they think. Polling suggests that a clear majority of Britons view Brexit as both a failure and a mistake in the first place, with similar support for rejoining the EU, although this depends in part on the pre-conditions for doing so.

This is a product of both lived experience and what pollsters delicately call “demographic churn” – that is, the death of many of the disproportionately older Britons who voted leave and their replacement on the electoral rolls by younger people with more positive views about the EU.

after newsletter promotion

Closer EU ties will give UK say on Brussels decisions, says Ed Miliband

Read more

A new constituency-level poll on Brexit sentiment found that hundreds of previously leave-backing areas, including Burnham’s Makerfield seat, now support rejoining.

Of the 632 Commons seats in England, Scotland and Wales, it found that voters in 512 would rejoin the EU, with 47 too close to call. Just 73 areas – slightly over 11% of the total – still want to stay out.

For the Conservatives, the battle has not ended. Badenoch will lambast the PM when he sets out his new EU deal in parliament on Monday. Her deputy, Alex Burghart, has already promised that a future Tory government would unpick it.

But make no mistake, Europe is no longer the Conservatives’ defining political thread, and division, as it was for several decades. May might, understandably, be unable to move on from the issue that made her PM and then destroyed her career. But her party, like the country, has no choice.
